architecture.mechanism: A fully discharged 12 V lead-acid battery cannot deliver the 200–600 A cold-crank burst because its terminal voltage collapses below the ~9–10 V needed by the starter solenoid and ECU boot loads; the architecture exploits a partitioned energy reserve — quiescent/parasitic loads are confined to the main battery while a high-power-density reserve (supercapacitor bank) is charged only when the alternator runs and then held in isolation, so it retains cranking capability even when the main battery is fully flat.
architecture.intervention: Add an isolated 12 V supercapacitor reserve module (≈500–1000 F, 16 V rating) wired through a threshold-controlled isolator: charge it from the alternator bus only above 13.5 V, disconnect it from the main bus when main voltage sags below 10.8 V, and on a key-on/crank request switch it directly onto the starter solenoid input, bypassing the depleted main battery; pair this with a low-voltage disconnect (≈11.5 V) for non-essential quiescent loads so the main battery is never drained past recovery by keyless-entry/immobilizer/keep-alive draws.
architecture.expected_effect: With the main battery discharged to ≤10.0 V, the engine still cranks and starts within 1–3 s; the factory 12 V bus is supported during cranking by the reserve; the reserve retains ≥80 % of its cold-crank capability after 30 days of vehicle inactivity at 25 °C, and the factory alternator and wiring remain the primary energy path with no change to OEM starting behavior.
architecture.falsification_test: Cheapest kill test: bench-measure the reserve bank's self-discharge over 30 days (leakage current vs. temperature), then compute retained energy against the engine's cold-crank energy requirement; if retained energy at −18 °C after 30 days is below the 0.5–3 s cranking demand, or if a full main-battery discharge to 10.0 V fails to produce a start, the architecture is falsified.
